member.name: T:DotNetCore.HayateOP.HayateNamedPoolCollection`1
member.summary: Holds every named pool of one element type: the lazily built singletons behind the declarations in the container.
member.remarks:
A pool is built on the first request for its name and then reused, so declaring a pool costs nothing until something asks for it — and asking twice never builds twice. Names that were never requested stay unbuilt, which is what makes "declare a pool per tenant" affordable.
The collection owns the pools it built and disposes them when the container is disposed; a pool that was never requested is never created and therefore never disposed.

member.summary: A named-pool declaration: the service key a pool is addressed by, plus the delegate that builds it when it is first asked for.
member.remarks: Named pools are deliberately not built on Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection keyed services: those only exist in version 8.0 and later of the abstractions package, so a keyed registration would be unavailable to the net6.0 / net7.0 targets this library ships. A named pool is therefore declared as one instance of this type in the container — the container's own "many registrations of one service type" facility, available on every supported target — and collects them. The observable behavior is the same on net48 through net10.0: one lazily built singleton per (type, name).

member.name: T:DotNetCore.HayateOP.IHayateNamedPoolAccessor
member.summary: Resolves named pools — and the single unnamed pool of a type — from the container.
member.remarks:
A pool registered with RegisterHayatePool<T>() is resolvable as directly; that stops working as soon as a second pool of the same type exists, because there is then no longer one answer to "the pool of T". Named pools are addressed through this accessor instead, which is what a typed client uses and what an application asks when it wants a specific pool by name.
Resolution never creates a pool: it returns what was registered, and throws when the name was never registered. Run-time creation is 's job, so a typo in a pool name surfaces as an error rather than silently starting an unconfigured pool.

member.name: T:DotNetCore.HayateOP.Logging.HayateMicrosoftLoggerFactory
member.summary: A logger factory that gives every pool its own Microsoft.Extensions.Logging category.
member.remarks: Purpose: the container and configuration paths can register several pools of the same element type — the unnamed pool plus any number of named ones — and before 2.9 they handed every one of them a logger built from CreateLogger<T>(), which is a single category for all of them. Two named pools of MyConnection were therefore indistinguishable downstream: a per-pool log level, a filter or a sink had to be expressed against one shared category string. With this factory the category is the pool name — MyConnection for the unnamed pool and MyConnection:primary / MyConnection:replica for named ones — which is the same name the pool already reports in its own log lines, statistics and snapshots. Serilog, NLog and log4net all reach HayateOP through the Microsoft.Extensions.Logging bridge, so routing MEL by category routes every one of them. Category of the unnamed pool: it used to be Microsoft.Extensions.Logging's own choice for CreateLogger<T>() — the namespace-qualified display name of the element type — and is now the element type name, which is what has always documented. A host that configures a log level by the namespace-qualified name has to update that configuration; no code changes are needed. A null factory is accepted: the loggers then come from , not from a silent sink. A host that never registered an ILoggerFactory has not asked for logging to be off — it has asked for no logging provider, and answering that with silence makes a noisy pool indistinguishable from a quiet one. The built-in logger is also what a bare HayatePoolBuilder<T> resolves, so the container path and the builder path behave the same way on a host without Microsoft.Extensions.Logging. Pass this factory to HayatePoolBuilder<T>.WithLoggerFactory; an explicit WithLogger still wins over it.

member.remarks:
This is the container path for a pooled type that has no public parameterless constructor — new NpgsqlConnection(cs), new SmtpClient(host) — and for any policy that has to be told something the container knows. The factory runs once, when the pool is first resolved; the policy it returns is registered as a singleton, so it is shared by every pool of .
It wins over a policy registered earlier in the container, the way repeated registrations normally keep the last one. Registering the policy directly (services.AddSingleton<IHayateObjectPolicy<T>>(sp => ...)) works too and needs no HayateOP call — both routes end in the same place.

member.summary: The body both RegisterHayatePool overloads share: one options registration, one pool registry, one object policy and one pool.
member.remarks: The policy registration deliberately differs between the two callers. A factory the caller passed explicitly is appended (AddSingleton), so it wins over anything registered earlier, matching the "last declaration wins" rule repeated registrations follow. The built-in default only fills the gap (TryAddSingleton), so a policy registered directly in the container is honoured instead of being silently replaced by the library's own — before 2.9 the default was appended unconditionally, which made registering a policy yourself an order-dependent no-op.
